1:
The fountain is identified almost unanimously, and the range of older opinions is worth recording. Gill lists them: two Jewish commentators take the verse literally, a third figuratively, and the Targum makes the fountain the doctrine of the law lying open as a spring; he would rather have it of the preaching of the Gospel, better of Christ himself, and best of all of his blood. He explains why blood should be called a fountain, not for the quantity shed but for its efficacy, being the blood of the Son of God, and why opened, since it is not sealed but stands always open, so that nothing hinders any from coming to it. Henry connects it with the piercing named in the previous chapter, from which came blood and water, both for cleansing; those who look on Christ pierced and mourn for the sins that pierced him may look again and rejoice, since it pleased the Lord to smite this rock that it might be a fountain of living waters. Wesley catches the same contrast in a phrase, that the spouse is to Christ a fountain sealed while Christ is to sinners a fountain opened.

Calvin sets the verse in its argument. Zechariah had promised the spirit of repentance to the people, but sorrow alone would not have been enough without God becoming propitious, so that having declared how bitterly they would grieve for having as it were pierced God, he now names the fruit of that repentance, which is washing. Calvin sees an allusion to the legal rites, since many washings were prescribed and to wash was the remedy for defilement, though water was of no value to cleanse the heart, the true ablution being by the blood shed for us. He canvasses the interpreters, some of whom made the fountain baptism, while others with more wisdom took it for the blood of Christ, and another for the grace of God flowing through the merits of the Redeemer; and he notes an observation that the word fountain itself intimates the perennity and abundance of that grace.

Clarke reads the recipients of the promise as the hardest test of it. The house of David means David's family and such persons as it included, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem such persons as that city held in its last days, when they clamoured for the blood of Christ; learn from this, he says, for whom Christ shed his blood. These were the worst of the human race, who rejected and slew him and afterwards persecuted his followers, and for these he died, so that none need despair. He also observes that the chapter continues the one before it and should not have been separated from it.

The promise that follows is set in a time none of them agree on. Gill argues that it refers neither to the Babylonish captivity and the return, after which idolatry ceased among that people, nor to the times of Christ, soon after which the lying oracles of the heathen ceased and paganism fell, but to a later conversion still to come. Keil and Delitzsch reads it structurally, taking the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem for the whole nation and this verse as beginning a description of the new life in fellowship with God that follows the cleansing. Clarke thinks the prophecy an ancient one, delivered while idolatry still had power in Israel and Judah, and takes the promise to mean that the very names of the idols shall be forgotten or held in such abhorrence that none will mention them; the prophets meant are all false teachers. Ellicott adds only that this is the single passage in the Old Testament where the phrase unclean spirit occurs, though it is frequent in the New. Wesley identifies the spirit flatly as the devil who sets the false prophets to work.
3:
The parents who kill their own son are explained as the swing of a reaction. Ellicott puts it as a movement of the whole people: the reaction from superstition would be scepticism, so that they would no longer believe in prophecy at all, and the very parents of a prophet would slay him as an impostor even though not legally convicted of falsehood. Clarke says only that the horror of the evil would be such that there would be no toleration of it. Gill takes it as an attempt to propagate idolatrous principles after they had been abundantly exposed. Wesley alone softens it, taking the father and mother for his dearest friends and the thrusting through for wounding, a chastisement with stripes that might leave marks behind; and the reading matters, since it decides what the wounds later in the passage are.

The garment is treated as a professional disguise. Clarke describes it, a rough garment of goats' hair, coarse wool or the coarse pile of the camel, the ordinary dress of God's prophets, which the false prophets wore too since they pretended to the same gifts and spirit; John Baptist, he notes, had a garment of this kind. Wesley says the same in a line. Gill turns to the shame rather than the dress, the man ashamed of doctrines that will appear to all men ridiculous and absurd. Ellicott marks the turn in the passage, that the prophet now reverts to those who are really false prophets.

The disclaimer that follows is read as an evasion under questioning. Clarke supplies the situation: a false diviner has been obliged to give up his practice and become a labourer, and being known for what he was he is questioned to see whether he is still addicted in heart to the same practices; he answers that he is no prophet at all, neither true nor false, but a husbandman brought up a herdsman. Ellicott would render the last clause not that a man taught him but that a man acquired or bought him, so that he pretends to be a purchased slave kept hard at work and with no leisure for professing inspiration; his meaning, he observes, is very different from that of the earlier prophet who used similar words in earnest. Gill has him disclaiming his order and laying aside his habit.

The wounds in his hands are the crux, and four answers are given. Gill offers three at once, the marks his parents left when they thrust him through, a mark received on entering an order, or stripes he had given himself in the exercise of his own will worship. Clarke takes them for marks received in honour of his idols, which the man excuses by saying he got them at home, where the idols had most probably been dedicated. Ellicott would render the preposition between rather than in, meaning on the hands and up the arms, and takes the questioner to be accusing him of cutting himself in idolatrous worship; on the answer he weighs two readings, that the friends are his false gods and he confesses with shame to having cut himself for them, which the passive verb is against, or better that the marks are stripes received in loving chastisement at home, as Wesley also takes them. In any case, Ellicott says, the man is anxious to disavow any pretence to prophecy; and he adds that throughout these passages the phrase that day covers a considerable period whose limits are hidden even from the prophet himself.

Clarke closes with a protest. He does not think these words are spoken at all concerning Jesus Christ; he has heard them quoted so, and cannot hear such an application without horror. In quoting from the Old Testament in reference to the New, he says, we cannot be too cautious, since we may wound the truth instead of honouring it.
7:
The sword and the shepherd are identified first. Gill rejects an older suggestion that the shepherd is Judas Maccabeus, slain in battle, and takes the words for the Father's concerning his Son, called my Shepherd because God has a property in him as well as in the flock. On the sword he offers several senses, the sorrows that pierced Christ's soul, the violent death he was put to, or rather the glittering sword of justice drawn against him and sheathed in him. Henry takes the same view of the speaker, the Father commissioning the sword of his justice to awake against his Son when he had voluntarily made his soul an offering for sin. Clarke adds why the sword is told to wake, since it had seemed long asleep and should long ago have struck either man or his substitute; and he calls the address a fine personification, setting beside it a passage of Aeschylus in which iron is a cruel umpire dividing a contested realm and allotting each claimant no wider a domain than his own body covers. Wesley reads the sword more broadly, of afflictions, persecutions and the cross.

The title given to the shepherd draws the closest work. Henry distinguishes two relations: as God he is God's fellow, having thought it no robbery to be equal with God, and as Mediator he is the Shepherd who undertook to feed the flock and lay down his life for the sheep. Clarke renders the phrase the strong man or the hero that is with me, and glosses it my neighbour. Ellicott notes the word occurs elsewhere only in the law and means either neighbour or the relation of fellowship, and puts it to a critical use: the foolish shepherd of the earlier chapter could hardly be called by the Lord the man of his fellowship, which he treats as conclusive against moving this passage back there. He offers two further arguments the same way, the similarity between the third part here and the half of the city in the next chapter, and the sense in which the word for land is used. Wesley states the doctrine plainly, that this speaks Christ, man with us and God with his Father, God and man in one person.

The smiting is described for what kind of death it makes. Henry presses the distinction: if he will be a sacrifice he must be slain, since without shedding of blood there is no remission, and the charge is given not to a rod to correct but to a sword to slay, and not to the sword of war, that he might die in the bed of honour, but to the sword of justice, that he might die as a criminal upon an ignominious tree. Ellicott supplies the human agency, that wicked men are the Lord's sword and through them his determinate counsel was executed, and states the ground, that the smiting was on account of the sin of the flock; the shepherd must be the same who is earlier represented as insulted and rejected. Clarke notes that our Lord quoted the second clause of his disciples, who were scattered at his crucifixion, every one giving up all for lost and going to his own house.

The little ones at the end are read as promise, not threat. Clarke takes the turning of the hand as care for the little flock, preserved from malice and persecution, and observes that it was wondrously preserved and has been increasing from year to year to the present day. Ellicott agrees that the hand is turned in merciful chastisement, and notes that the word for the little ones occurs only here in this form and means perhaps the humble and patient, denoting those afterwards called the third part. Wesley says the same, that God turns his hand in favour and protection, to keep the new and weak disciples.
8:
Where the two parts are cut off, and when, is answered differently by every voice. Gill reports one commentator who confines it to the land of Israel and another who extends it to all the world, and takes the wider sense himself; he denies that the prophecy refers to the calamities at the destruction of Jerusalem, when a few were saved as a remnant according to the election of grace, and applies it instead to the state of the church and its troubles at a later day. Ellicott keeps the narrower sense of the word, of the land of Israel. Clarke fixes it historically in the war with the Romans, and reads the surviving third as those who believed on the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom not one perished in the siege or in the wars that followed. Wesley cautions that the fraction is not exact, only that the greater part should die, whether by the sword or in unbelief, while a lesser part should escape.

Keil and Delitzsch reads these two verses as the explanation of the promise about the little ones in the verse before. The word used there occurs nowhere else in that form and is synonymous with the ordinary word for the small, taken figuratively of the miserable, the same as those called the poor of the flock in an earlier chapter; from which it follows that they are not identical with the whole flock but form a small portion of it, the poor and righteous in the nation who suffer injustice. He quotes another writer to the same effect, that the assertion that the flock will be scattered while God brings back his hand to the small ones plainly implies that these are one portion of the entire flock, for which God prepares a different fate from the larger whole about to be dispersed. On the fulfilment he points to the gospel narratives, where the bringing back of the hand was realized first of all in the case of the apostles.

The refining of the surviving third is where the three readings of the chapter meet. Gill takes the fire for tribulation, as the Targum explains it, or great distresses comparable to fire, and lists what he means, the hour of temptation, the time of trouble such as there never was since there was a nation, and the time of the slaying of the witnesses. Clarke reads it of the Christian church, which shall endure a great fight of afflictions by which it is refined and not consumed, and traces the sequence of the verse: in that way they offer all their prayers and supplications to God, and by the answer communion is established between God and them for ever, so that there shall be a general restoration. Ellicott is the most guarded of the three. Amid all the calamities, a remnant should be saved and purified, and in the light of the Gospel these words may, if they are retained in their present context, be understood as fulfilled in those who embraced Christianity; but the prophet, standing where he does, speaks vaguely, and by the analogy of the captivity that had already passed.
